title: Reformers commonly reject the Latria–Dulia split, because one cult is properly religious and Scripture mixes the words
source_text: XVIII. Caeterum vulgatam distinctionem cultus Religiosi in Latriam & Duliam communiter improbant Scholae Reformatae Doctores. Idque duplici nomine. Et primo quidem, quoniam unicus est cultus qui proprie & simpliciter Religiosus dici mereatur: nempe, cultus qui Deo proprius est. Ille vero qui creaturis, etiam praestantissimis & sanctissimis, defertur, religiosus dici nequit, nisi improprie & aequivoce. Deinde quia in Scripturae usu saepius confunduntur Latriae & Dulia voces. Siquidem apud Graecos interpretes Veteris Testamenti λατρείαν aliquando de servitio humano usurpatur: frequenter vero δουλείαν tam in Veteri quam in Novo Testamento ad solum cultum divinum restringitur.
pass_a_gloss: But the doctors of the Reformed School commonly disapprove the vulgar distinction of religious cult into Latria and Dulia. And that on two accounts. First, because there is one cult only which deserves to be called religious properly and simply: namely the cult proper to God. But that which is paid to creatures, even the most excellent and holy, cannot be called religious except improperly and equivocally. Second, because in the use of Scripture the words Latria and Dulia are quite often confused. For among the Greek interpreters of the Old Testament latreia is sometimes used of human service, while douleia is frequently restricted, both in the Old and in the New Testament, to the divine cult alone.
pass_b_english: Reformed doctors generally reject dividing religious cult into Latria and Dulia.
Only the cult proper to God deserves the name religious in the proper and simple sense; creature-honor is religious only improperly.
Scripture also mixes the words: latreia sometimes means human service, and douleia is often kept for God's cult alone.

choices.why: The Greek usage is the second reason the distinction fails.
rejected: dulia as a biblical technical term
